description: We're a team from Raipur building for NASA Space Apps 2026's challenge "Abandoned but Not Forgotten." We want to turn the equipment NASA left on the Moon and Mars into stories that make space history personal, using data, visuals and narrative. Our skills: [your skills, e.g., coding, data analysis]. Looking for teammates in writing, graphic design, web development or data visualization, and anyone who loves space history!
summary:
Last Known Position is an interactive space archive that helps people meet the machines humanity left behind on the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Visitors fly through a live 3D solar system, explore real Moon and Mars maps, and open story dossiers for 32 landers, rovers, spacecraft, and scientific instruments.

Every artifact has a last known position, mission facts, a real image, sources, a live “silence” counter, and an imagined first-person log clearly labeled as fact-based fiction. The project turns NASA data into an approachable story for young learners while still providing sources and deeper context for older audiences. It shows that “abandoned” hardware is also scientific heritage: Apollo mirrors still return laser signals, Mars rovers revealed ancient water, and distant spacecraft continue carrying humanity’s message outward.
details:
Last Known Position makes NASA’s discarded and retired exploration hardware feel present rather than forgotten. The experience is organized into Moon, Mars, Deep Space, Silence Board, Timeline, Quiz, and About sections.

The core feature is an interactive 3D solar-system simulator. It places planets on their computed positions for a selected date and lets visitors fly to the Moon, Mars, Ceres, Eros, or spacecraft including Voyager, Pioneer, New Horizons, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, and Kepler. On the Moon and Mars, glowing, accessible map pins lead to 32 artifact dossiers. Each dossier includes a public-domain NASA image, mission facts, dates, current status, a sourced narrative, what the mission taught us, a timeline, and an explicitly labeled imagined log based on real mission facts.

The project was designed for ages 10–14, classrooms, and casual space fans. It uses short, readable language, read-aloud controls, keyboard navigation, visible focus states, reduced-motion support, high-contrast day mode, and map/list alternatives so exploration does not depend on dragging or 3D interaction.

Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js, and Leaflet. NASA/JPL orbital data drives the simulator; LROC coordinates and NASA Trek maps place hardware on the Moon and Mars. The project is creative because it treats each object’s “last known position” as both a scientific location and an emotional starting point for storytelling.

AI assistance was used for coding, debugging, research organization, and text editing. All mission facts, dates, coordinates, and source links were independently checked against the cited NASA, JPL, LROC, and NSSDCA resources.
